title: Dependency hygiene when exploits land in weeks
author: Conor Bronsdon
summary: Dan Lorenc, co-founder and CEO of Chainguard, argues that average time to exploit has gone negative. He is explicit that the figure is not his data. He points to independent reports from Mandiant, CrowdStrike, and other vulnerability detection and response vendors. The glossary defines the calculation as exploitation date minus a chosen reference date (Mandiant's 2023 analysis uses patch release), so a negative average places observed exploitation before the patch release, on average. It is an average over observed exploited vulnerabilities, not a promise about your patching window. Dan's theory of the distribution is a separate claim. Dan notes that exploitation before disclosure, the zero-day case, has always existed. He thinks the long tail got squeezed: flaws disclosed and never exploited, or exploited years later. Weaponizing a write-up, in his account, is now cheap. Anybody with a cheap model, anybody with an open model can take the knowledge of a vulnerability and build a POC or build an exploit for it in minutes. Dan Lorenc, co-founder and CEO of Chainguard, on Chain of Thought ep 68 He adds that you are only limited by token cost. He describes the old pattern, people crawling a backlog and exploiting a chosen bug 180 or 270 days later, as over if the bug will be exploited at all. In that case he expects weeks. I treat that as a dependency problem you can work before a report arrives. If a known bug can become an exploit in minutes, every library you cannot name, rebuild, or delete is time you do not have. What should you record before an upgrade has to happen tomorrow? Dan's advice to a maintainer of small open source projects and to an enterprise security leader is the same practice at different scale. He wants you to be able to upgrade any dependency if a patch lands tomorrow, and he uses Log4j as the drill. Just imagine what happened during Log4j and then go make a list of every dependency you have and kind of game plan it out. Dan Lorenc, co-founder and CEO of Chainguard, on Chain of Thought ep 68 I would keep that list in version control. For each direct dependency, record the pinned version, the date you pinned it, whether you can rebuild it from source you have, whether a maintainer will take a patch, and what breaks if you remove it. Then repeat the pass for indirect dependencies: Dan points out that the newest release of a library you chose can still depend on something five years old. He puts open source at anywhere from 90 to 95 percent of a modern application by line of code, with many applications sharing that same code. When models are aimed at a running app, he says they find issues in your own code, in third-party code, and often in a chain across both. He also says vulnerability databases mostly deal with flaws still present in the latest version. If the bug is gone upstream and nobody filed it, a scanner that only trusts those signals will not tell you to move. Some dangerous code was removed upstream on purpose with no vulnerability ID, or disappeared in a refactor, so there is no patch to copy. Two more columns belong on the list for that reason: "present in the latest version?" and "can we reach a maintainer?" Dan's view is that a maintainer has no duty to handle a security report. Say whether you will, and how. If you will not, expect a fork. He thinks the cost of keeping a fork has dropped because agents are good at rebasing and merge conflicts, the work that used to make long-lived forks a bad trade. This checker is a sketch of that rule. It is not a scanner Dan or Chainguard runs. # Sketch only. Illustrates an inventory rule. from datetime import date MAX_AGE_DAYS = 365 * 2 def flag ( dep ): age = ( date . today () - dep [ " pinned_on " ]). days reasons = [] if dep [ " indirect " ] and age > MAX_AGE_DAYS : reasons . append ( " old indirect pin " ) if not dep [ " rebuildable_from_source " ]: reasons . append ( " cannot rebuild from source " ) if dep [ " unused " ]: reasons . append ( " candidate to remove " ) if dep [ " we_ship_it " ] and not dep [ " maintainer_reachable " ]: reasons . append ( " plan a fork or a replacement " ) return reasons When do you trim, rebuild, or remove a package? I would start by cutting packages, then by rebuilding what remains from source into a smaller image. Dan asks whether you need 17 database drivers or one shared choice. Fewer libraries means fewer things that can page the whole team. For what you keep, I want the artifact to contain only packages you can reproduce from source you have read, not a base image full of tools the process never calls. When a fix would change behavior so much that an in-place patch is the wrong move, Dan says it is often easier to upgrade away from the component or remove it. He expects more projects to delete legacy behavior on purpose. After Log4j, he says, a lot of Java projects removed remote JNDI code even without a filed vulnerability in that specific tree. On Log4j itself, he calls the upstream response an open source success, with fixes shipped in days; knowing where it ran and applying the updates took months to years. He calls patching a treadmill you never finish. I would rather shrink the treadmill: pay down the dependencies you cannot upgrade, and delete classes of behavior you do not need. What should you fuzz in code you own? Fuzzing is Dan's older case of discovery running ahead of fixes. You point generated or mutated inputs at a program, often a parser, and see what crashes. A finding is a starting point: you still reproduce it, find the cause, judge the security impact, and test a fix. But in the Linux kernel and a bunch of other critical projects, fuzzing has been outpacing remediation for a decade already. Dan Lorenc, co-founder and CEO of Chainguard, on Chain of Thought ep 68 He describes Google's OSS-Fuzz program as constantly sending random inputs into programs and looking for crashes. Once you have a crash, you can usually learn why. The bottleneck he names is the fix, not the search. He thinks AI is the first real chance to speed up the fixing. I would fuzz the parsers and decoders in code I maintain, including the small libraries I have decided to keep, and I would schedule the triage in the same week as the run. A crash with no owner is another row in a queue. Dan's point about model reports is similar: one run against a sandboxed app, with source and debugging tools and a goal like "break this app," can return many paths. Fixing a single link may not stop the next run from finding another chain. Split the report into patchable pieces, de-duplicate, and decide which bugs are yours. When does a package change need a compliance check? A dependency diff can also be a data-flow diff. Continuous compliance swaps a point-in-time audit for live monitoring, because fields that trip no rule on their own can become identifiable when combined, long after someone signed off. I would run that check on each dependency change: what the package reads, where it sends that data, and whether the new combination is identifiable. If you cannot answer, do not ship the bump. Checklist Keep a diffable inventory of direct and indirect dependencies: version, pin date, rebuild-from-source, maintainer reach, and whether the issue exists in the latest upstream. For each package, choose remove, rebuild from source into a smaller image, or keep with an upgrade you could run tomorrow. Fuzz parsers you own, then reproduce and judge security impact before you call the crash done. On each dependency or data-join change, check whether new combinations create a privacy obligation after the last audit. When you cite a time-to-exploit number, write down the reference date, and do not treat one vendor average as your patch window. title: AI agents on WhatsApp: how to automate sales and support without losing the human touch
author: Sebastián Duque
summary: In short: an AI agent on WhatsApp answers, qualifies and serves your customers 24/7 using your business's real information (catalog, prices, inventory, calendar, order status) and hands the conversation to a person when needed. Built well, it cuts response times from hours to seconds and frees your team from repetitive questions. Built badly, it makes up answers and burns your customer relationships. The difference comes down to three things: connected data, clear limits and human handoff. Chatbot vs. AI agent: not the same thing Traditional chatbots run on menus and buttons: "type 1 for sales, 2 for support". They work for simple flows but break as soon as a customer writes something unexpected. An AI agent understands natural language, keeps the context of the conversation and, above all, can take action : check inventory, send a quote, book an appointment, create an order or look up a shipment by connecting to your systems. Menu chatbot AI agent Understands free text and voice notes No Yes Keeps context Limited Yes, throughout the conversation Queries your systems Rarely Yes: CRM, inventory, calendar, payments Takes actions No Yes, with rules and permissions Escalates to a person Manually Automatically, with a case summary What can an AI agent do on WhatsApp? Sales Answer questions about products, prices and availability with real-time data. Qualify leads (budget, need, urgency) and pass the best ones to your sales team. Send quotes and payment links. Follow up on abandoned carts or quotes. Customer support Resolve FAQs without waiting: opening hours, policies, warranties, shipping. Look up the status of an order or case with an ID number. Take complaints, classify them and open a ticket in your system. Operations Book, confirm and reschedule appointments or reservations. Send reminders and confirmations. Collect documents or data for internal processes. How it works under the hood A serious agent has several parts working together: Official WhatsApp Business API: the Meta-approved connection, with a verified number and message templates. Avoid unofficial solutions that put your number at risk. Language model: the "brain" that understands the customer and writes the replies. Your business knowledge (RAG): documents, catalog and policies indexed so the agent answers with your information instead of guesses. We explain it in our guide to AI for business . Tools and integrations: functions the agent can use, like checking inventory, creating orders or booking, each with defined permissions. Rules and limits: what it can promise, what it can't, when it must escalate and which data it must never ask for. A dashboard for your team: where you see conversations, step in whenever you want and measure results. The mistakes we see most Letting the model improvise: without connected knowledge, the agent invents prices, policies or availability. That leads to complaints and lost trust. No human handoff: a frustrated customer who can't reach a person goes to the competition. Using unofficial numbers or APIs: risk of the number being banned and losing every conversation. Ignoring privacy: requesting or storing personal data without consent or security measures, in breach of data protection laws. Not measuring: without metrics you don't know whether the agent sells more or just replies more. How much does it cost and what return can you expect? The cost has three parts: implementation (flow design, integrations, knowledge and testing), AI model usage (paid by conversation volume) and WhatsApp Business fees , which Meta charges by message type and country. Check the current rates in Meta's official documentation, since they change periodically. To estimate the return, measure before and after: Average first response time. Share of conversations resolved without human intervention. Conversion rate from conversations to sales or appointments. Team hours freed up for higher-value work. How to implement it step by step Pick one concrete use case: for example, FAQs and booking. Don't try to automate everything in the first month. Organize your information: catalog, prices, policies and approved answers. Define limits and escalation: what the agent handles and when a person steps in. Integrate your systems: CRM, inventory, calendar or payments, with least-privilege permissions. Test with real conversations: before launch, with your team playing the difficult customer. Launch, measure and improve: review conversations every week and adjust knowledge and rules. How we do it at Key Lab We design AI agents connected to each company's real systems, using the official WhatsApp API, verified knowledge, clear business rules, human handoff and a metrics dashboard. And because we're a software engineering studio, when the agent needs an integration that doesn't exist, we build it. Frequently asked questions Does the agent replace my support team? No. It handles the repetitive work and the hours when nobody's available, and passes your team the conversations that need human judgment, already summarized. Can it understand WhatsApp voice notes? Yes. Voice notes can be transcribed and processed as text, which is key in markets where customers prefer sending audio. What if the agent doesn't know the answer? It should say so honestly and escalate to a person, never make something up. That rule is designed and tested before launch. Can I use my current WhatsApp number? In most cases yes, by migrating it to the official WhatsApp Business API. The migration needs planning because it changes how the number is used. title: Performance no .NET com IA: medir, otimizar e provar com BenchmarkDotNet
author: Henrique Mauri
summary: A IA virou uma ótima companheira para revisar código. Peça para ela "melhorar a performance" de um método e, em segundos, você recebe uma lista de sugestões escritas com total confiança: use Span<T> , troque LINQ por for , adicione stackalloc , paralelize com Parallel.ForEach . O problema é que confiança não é medição. Boa parte dessas sugestões não muda nada, algumas pioram e outras mudam o comportamento do sistema sem ninguém perceber. Neste artigo, vou mostrar o método que uso para otimizar código .NET com ajuda da IA: medir antes, otimizar uma mudança por vez e provar depois . Tudo com um exemplo real, que saiu de 1,5 segundo para 12 milissegundos e de 33 MB para 0,23 MB de alocação . O cenário Um relatório de vendas comum: recebemos linhas de pedidos no formato PEDIDO;CLIENTE;SKU;QUANTIDADE;PRECO , somamos o total por cliente, ignoramos clientes bloqueados e retornamos os 10 maiores. Esta é a versão original. Ela funciona, é legível e passaria tranquilamente em muitos code reviews: public static List < ItemRelatorio > Gerar ( string [] linhas , List < string > clientesBloqueados ) { var pedidos = new List < Pedido >(); foreach ( var linha in linhas ) { var partes = linha . Split ( ';' ); pedidos . Add ( new Pedido ( Numero : partes [ 0 ], Cliente : partes [ 1 ], Sku : partes [ 2 ], Quantidade : int . Parse ( partes [ 3 ], CultureInfo . InvariantCulture ), PrecoUnitario : decimal . Parse ( partes [ 4 ], CultureInfo . InvariantCulture ))); } var resultado = new List < ItemRelatorio >(); foreach ( var cliente in pedidos . Select ( p => p . Cliente ). Distinct ()) { if ( clientesBloqueados . Contains ( cliente )) continue ; var total = pedidos . Where ( p => p . Cliente == cliente ) . Sum ( p => p . Quantidade * p . PrecoUnitario ); resultado . Add ( new ItemRelatorio ( cliente , total )); } return resultado . OrderByDescending ( r => r . Total ) . ThenBy ( r => r . Cliente , StringComparer . Ordinal ) . Take ( 10 ) . ToList (); } Com 100 mil linhas e 1.000 clientes, esse método leva mais de 1,5 segundo . Se você já sabe onde está o problema, ótimo. Mas o ponto aqui é o método, não o palpite. Passo 1: medir antes de tocar no código Antes de pedir qualquer coisa para a IA, crie um benchmark com o BenchmarkDotNet . Ele cuida de aquecimento, múltiplas execuções e estatística, coisas que um Stopwatch solto não resolve: [ MemoryDiagnoser ] public class RelatorioBenchmark { private string [] _linhas = []; private List < string > _bloqueadosLista = []; private HashSet < string > _bloqueadosSet = []; [ Params ( 10_000 , 100_000 )] public int Linhas { get ; set ; } [ GlobalSetup ] public void Setup () { _linhas = GeradorDeDados . GerarLinhas ( Linhas , clientes : 1_000 , seed : 42 ); _bloqueadosLista = GeradorDeDados . GerarBloqueados ( 50 ); _bloqueadosSet = new HashSet < string >( _bloqueadosLista , StringComparer . Ordinal ); } [ Benchmark ( Baseline = true )] public List < ItemRelatorio > Original () => RelatorioOriginal . Gerar ( _linhas , _bloqueadosLista ); [ Benchmark ] public List < ItemRelatorio > Otimizado () => RelatorioOtimizado . Gerar ( _linhas , _bloqueadosSet ); } Dois detalhes importantes: o [MemoryDiagnoser] mostra quanto cada execução aloca de memória (em APIs com muita carga, alocação vira pressão no Garbage Collector), e o benchmark só vale em Release . Passo 2: dar contexto para a IA, não só o código A diferença entre uma sugestão genérica e uma análise útil está no contexto. No repositório, deixo um arquivo CLAUDE.md com as regras de performance do projeto: ## Regras para otimizações de performance - Nunca otimize sem medir antes. Todo gargalo precisa de um benchmark no BenchmarkDotNet. - Proponha uma mudança por vez e explique a complexidade (Big O) antes e depois. - O comportamento não pode mudar: a validação em Program.cs precisa continuar passando. - Considere alocações de memória, não só tempo ([MemoryDiagnoser]). - Não use unsafe, stackalloc ou paralelismo sem um benchmark que justifique. E o pedido para a IA vai junto com o resultado do benchmark: Analise o método RelatorioOriginal.Gerar. Segue o resultado do BenchmarkDotNet. Liste as hipóteses de gargalo ordenadas por impacto estimado, com a complexidade de cada trecho. Proponha UMA mudança por vez. O resultado do relatório precisa continuar idêntico. Repare que não pedi "deixe mais rápido". Pedi hipóteses ordenadas, complexidade e uma mudança por vez. A IA responde muito melhor quando o pedido tem critério. O que a análise encontrou Três problemas, em ordem de impacto: Complexidade O(clientes × pedidos). Para cada cliente distinto, o Where percorre todos os pedidos de novo. Com 1.000 clientes e 100 mil pedidos, são cerca de 100 milhões de comparações para algo que pode ser feito em uma única passada. List.Contains para os bloqueados. Cada consulta é uma busca linear. Com um HashSet , a busca passa a ser O(1). Split em todas as linhas. Cada Split cria um array e uma string por campo, inclusive para campos que nem usamos, como número do pedido e SKU. Passo 3: uma mudança por vez, medindo cada uma Aqui está a parte que mais gente pula. Aplicar tudo de uma vez até funciona, mas você não sabe qual mudança trouxe o ganho, e fica impossível justificar a complexidade extra de cada uma. Etapa 1: uma única passada com Dictionary . Em vez de agrupar depois, acumulamos o total por cliente enquanto lemos as linhas. O algoritmo cai de O(clientes × pedidos) para O(pedidos). Etapa 2: HashSet para os bloqueados. Uma linha de mudança, ganho garantido. Etapa 3: parsing com ReadOnlySpan<char> e busca sem alocar strings. Em vez de Split , percorremos a linha como um span. E com o alternate lookup , disponível a partir do .NET 9, conseguimos consultar o HashSet e o Dictionary usando o próprio span, sem criar uma string para cada linha: public static List < ItemRelatorio > Gerar ( string [] linhas , HashSet < string > clientesBloqueados ) { if (! clientesBloqueados . TryGetAlternateLookup < ReadOnlySpan < char >>( out var bloqueados )) throw new ArgumentException ( "Crie o HashSet com StringComparer.Ordinal." , nameof ( clientesBloqueados )); var totais = new Dictionary < string , decimal >( StringComparer . Ordinal ); var totaisPorCliente = totais . GetAlternateLookup < ReadOnlySpan < char >>(); foreach ( var linha in linhas ) { // Formato: PEDIDO;CLIENTE;SKU;QUANTIDADE;PRECO ReadOnlySpan < char > resto = linha ; ProximoCampo ( ref resto ); // número do pedido (não usado no relatório) var cliente = ProximoCampo ( ref resto ); ProximoCampo ( ref resto ); // SKU (não usado no relatório) var quantidade = int . Parse ( ProximoCampo ( ref resto ), NumberStyles . Integer , CultureInfo . InvariantCulture ); var preco = decimal . Parse ( resto , NumberStyles . Number , CultureInfo . InvariantCulture ); if ( bloqueados . Contains ( cliente )) continue ; // Busca pelo span: a string do cliente só é criada na primeira vez que ele aparece ref var total = ref CollectionsMarshal . GetValueRefOrAddDefault ( totaisPorCliente , cliente , out _ ); total += quantidade * preco ; } return totais . Select ( t => new ItemRelatorio ( t . Key , t . Value )) . OrderByDescending ( r => r . Total ) . ThenBy ( r => r . Cliente , StringComparer . Ordinal ) . Take ( 10 ) . ToList (); } private static ReadOnlySpan < char > ProximoCampo ( ref ReadOnlySpan < char > resto ) { var fim = resto . IndexOf ( ';' ); var campo = resto [.. fim ]; resto = resto [( fim + 1 )..]; return campo ; } O CollectionsMarshal.GetValueRefOrAddDefault devolve uma referência direta para o valor dentro do dicionário. Assim, fazemos a busca e a atualização em uma única operação, em vez de buscar, somar e gravar de novo. Repare também no que não mudou: o LINQ no final continua lá. Ele roda sobre 1.000 itens, não sobre 100 mil. LINQ não é o vilão. Algoritmo ruim é. Passo 4: provar Primeiro, garantir que nada quebrou. Antes de rodar o benchmark, o Program.cs compara o relatório de todas as versões com o original e interrompe a execução se houver qualquer diferença: var esperado = RelatorioOriginal . Gerar ( linhas , bloqueados ); var bloqueadosSet = new HashSet < string >( bloqueados , StringComparer . Ordinal ); var versoes = new [] { RelatorioEtapas . Etapa1UmaPassada ( linhas , bloqueados ), RelatorioEtapas . Etapa2HashSet ( linhas , bloqueadosSet ), RelatorioOtimizado . Gerar ( linhas , bloqueadosSet ) }; if ( versoes . Any ( v => ! esperado . SequenceEqual ( v ))) throw new InvalidOperationException ( "As versões produziram relatórios diferentes. A otimização mudou o comportamento." ); Depois, os números. Medições com 100 mil linhas e 1.000 clientes, no .NET 10: Versão Tempo médio Memória alocada Original 1.553 ms 33,1 MB Etapa 1: uma passada com Dictionary 40 ms 24,9 MB Etapa 2: HashSet para bloqueados 26 ms 24,9 MB Etapa 3: Span + alternate lookup 11,9 ms 0,23 MB Agora dá para enxergar o que cada mudança entregou: A Etapa 1 foi responsável por quase todo o ganho de tempo (de 1,5 s para 40 ms). Uma mudança de algoritmo, sem nenhuma técnica avançada. A Etapa 2 reduziu mais um terço do tempo com uma única linha alterada. A Etapa 3 praticamente zerou as alocações : de 25 MB para 0,23 MB. Em um método chamado milhares de vezes por minuto, isso significa muito menos trabalho para o Garbage Collector. Os valores absolutos vão mudar na sua máquina. As proporções, não. O repositório tem o BenchmarkDotNet configurado para você reproduzir. Onde a IA mais erra em performance Usando IA todos os dias, esses são os erros que mais vejo nas sugestões: Otimizar o que não é gargalo. Trocar o LINQ final por um for não muda nada quando ele roda sobre 1.000 itens. Micro-otimização antes do algoritmo. Span e stackalloc não salvam um código O(n²). Primeiro o algoritmo, depois as alocações. Mudar comportamento sem perceber. Remover o CultureInfo.InvariantCulture "para simplificar" quebra o parsing de 19.90 em um servidor configurado em português. Paralelizar por reflexo. Parallel.ForEach em um laço que já leva 12 ms costuma piorar o resultado e ainda introduz problemas de concorrência. Conclusão A IA acelera muito o trabalho de performance: encontra hipóteses em segundos, explica complexidade e escreve a primeira versão do código otimizado. Mas ela não substitui o método. Meça antes, peça com critério, mude uma coisa por vez e prove com números. É assim que a IA deixa de ser um gerador de palpites e vira uma ferramenta de engenharia. O código completo, com o benchmark, a validação e o CLAUDE.md , está no meu GitHub: github.com/hgmauri/sample-performance-ia E você, já pegou a IA sugerindo uma "otimização" que piorou o código? Conta nos comentários.
